extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, playwrights, and storytellers writing film/screenplays (professional and aspiring)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on research, creativity, scene-generation, and the conventions and mastery of film genres to design effective stories and screenplays. Covers sources of research (memory, imagination, fact), creative selection, genre taxonomy, genre-specific conventions, positioning audiences, and creative limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory (as research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lean back from your desk and ask, 'What do I know from personal experience that touches on my characters’ lives?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relive and vividly describe personal experiences (e.g., a childhood fear of being locked in a closet) to convert memory into 'working knowledge.' Write it down: in your head it’s memory, on the page it becomes usable material for honest, one-of-a-kind scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination (as research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lean back and ask, 'What would it be like to live my character’s life hour by hour, day by day?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch detailed, vivid fragments of everyday life (how characters shop, make love, pray). Use imagination to take slivers of dream/experience and seek hidden connections; write these envisioned scenes down. A 'working imagination' equals actionable research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact / Library Research
rubrics_metrics.description: When blocked or lacking something to say, go to the library: talent must be stimulated by facts and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research expands the circle of your experience, confirms universals (giving you an audience), and provides insights you couldn't reach alone. Research combats cliché and fear, provides factual grounding for genres (e.g., Domestic Drama), and feeds talent that otherwise can be starved by ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research must lead to events, not accumulation of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographical, psychological, physical, political, and historical research is essential but pointless if it doesn’t lead to the creation of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story is a design of events toward a meaningful climax; research is meat for imagination and invention, not the end. Avoid treating research as the story itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research must not become procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let study replace writing; too many talents spend years studying and never write anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origination and exploration go back and forth; don't postpone composition by endless research. Use research to stimulate writing, not to delay it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturation and the 'virgin birth' phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters ‘suddenly spring to life’ when a writer's knowledge reaches saturation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The impression that a story is writing itself marks the point where research, memory, and imagination have saturated the writer. This apparent spontaneity is the reward of sustained work, not mystical creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATIVITY = creative choices of inclusion and exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing requires inventing far more material than you can use, then astutely selecting moments true to character and world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create many alternative beats/scenes (five-to-one, ten-to-one, perhaps twenty-to-one). The craft is in choosing the best material; creative choices determine what to include and what to destroy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity-to-quality ratio (generate far more than you use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity is five to one, perhaps ten or twenty to one: invent far more material than you can possibly use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to generate many variants and then select the top ~10% of excellence. Rewriting should not be mere tinkering—discard the weaker material to leave every scene strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing clichés by exhaustive variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't trust first inspiration—sketch many different ways a scene could happen to avoid cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List dozens of variants of an obvious idea (e.g., how lovers meet). Ask: Which scene is truest to my characters? Truest to their world? Has never been onscreen quite this way before? Choose the variation that best satisfies these questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a cliché is right, reinvent its details through research
rubrics_metrics.description: If the clichéd setting is genuinely the truest expression of character, explore many variations within that setting to find an original truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct field research (hang out, observe, get involved) until you know the cliché world like no writer before you—then show the truth so audiences react with 'That’s right!' rather than boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre conventions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each genre imposes conventions of setting, role, event, and value that the audience expects and that shape what’s possible within a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify your genre, study its governing practices, and use conventions as creative limitations that inspire rather than stifle invention. Misuse or omission of conventions confuses audiences; use them to lead expectations to fresh moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disillusionment Plot conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary convention: protagonist opens optimistic; second convention: repeated negative story turns that poison dreams and end in cynicism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern (positive-to-negative worldview) defines the Disillusionment Plot and offers many paths to hopelessness—use conventions but vary the particulars to avoid cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime Genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a crime early in the telling; there must be a detective figure who discovers clues and suspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgenres vary by POV (murder mystery, caper, detective, gangster, thriller, courtroom, newspaper, espionage, prison drama, film noir). Use the required early crime and investigative mechanics to satisfy audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thriller convention: make it personal
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Thriller the criminal must 'make it personal' to deepen drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To deepen stakes, the criminal crosses the line (menaces the cop’s family or frames the cop). The story requires identification, apprehension, and punishment of the criminal to satisfy the genre's promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s overriding convention: nobody gets hurt
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy must reassure the audience that, however chaotic, characters ultimately are not hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a safety net so physical and emotional torments remain bearable. Black Comedy bends this rule, allowing sharper pain that still produces dark laughter; use subgenre conventions consciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Film conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Art Film conventions include absence of stars, production outside the Hollywood system, often non-English language, cerebral emphasis, and unconventionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art Film internal conventions favor mood, enigma, symbolism, unresolved tensions, and an ethic of unconventional structure (Minimalism, Antistructure). These external and internal features become marketing points and critical talking points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of genre (study method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To master a genre: list works like yours (successes and failures), watch films while following the screenplay, break films into setting/role/event/value, and stack analyses to find recurring conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume genre knowledge from casual viewing; systematic analysis (including failures) reveals what your genre always does so you can anticipate audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning the audience (marketing aligns expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful marketing positions the audience so they arrive with appropriate expectations formed by title, poster, and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you promise a genre (through promotion) you must deliver its conventions; mispositioning (e.g., marketing as a Murder Mystery when it's actually a Maturation Plot) causes confusion and poor word-of-mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Limitation (freedom within obstacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate limits (genre conventions, form constraints) provide the resistance that stimulates imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose self-limits (like a rhyme scheme) to force inventive solutions. Genre convention is a 'rhyme scheme' for storytellers: it inspires richer invention by constraining options in productive ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action/Adventure convention: hero-at-the-mercy scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief convention: the hero must be at the mercy of the villain and then turn the tables from helplessness to victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scene is imperative to test the protagonist's ingenuity and will. Because it’s often clichéd, seek fresh executions (examples: RAIDERS — gun; DIE HARD — gun duct-taped to back; MIDNIGHT RUN — riffing variations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre selection determines story possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of genre sharply determines and limits what’s possible within a story because design must envision and manipulate the audience’s learned anticipations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify genre early and research its conventions; genres supply both opportunity and constraint, guiding what events, roles, and values will feel coherent to an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, judgment, and will to prune failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius includes the power to create expressive beats and the judgment and will to weed out banalities, conceits, false notes, and lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expose every failure—omit weaker material. The writer must ruthlessly destroy what diminishes the work to leave only brilliant choices.
